title: Composite Pattern
summary: Treating a single object and a group of objects through the same interface — the pattern behind file trees, UI component trees, and org charts.

slides.markdown:
A **Composite** lets you treat a single object and a group of objects through the same interface, so client code doesn't need to know whether it's holding one leaf or an entire subtree.

Think of a file system: a file and a folder both support "get size" — a file returns its own byte count, a folder sums its children's sizes recursively, and the caller doesn't need an if-statement to tell which one it has. Composite is how you model any part-whole hierarchy — file trees, UI components, org charts — with one recursive interface.

slides.sectionTitle: The problem: treating a single object and a group of objects the same way
slides.markdown:
Without Composite, computing a folder's total size means checking: is this a `File` (return its size) or a `Folder` (loop over children, recursing for subfolders)? Every piece of code that walks the tree needs that same `isinstance` check, and every new node type (a symlink? a compressed archive?) means updating every one of those checks.

The deeper problem is conceptual: a single file and a directory tree containing a million files are being treated as different kinds of things, when for most operations — get size, get name, render — they should behave identically from the caller's point of view.

slides.sectionTitle: Composite: a tree of components sharing one interface (leaf + composite)
slides.markdown:
Composite defines one interface — say `FileSystemNode` with `get_size()` — that both a `File` (a *leaf*, no children) and a `Folder` (a *composite*, holds children) implement. `File.get_size()` returns its own byte count directly. `Folder.get_size()` sums `child.get_size()` over every child, calling the exact same method regardless of whether that child is a file or another folder.

The recursion falls out naturally: the caller calls `.get_size()` once, on the root, and the tree structure handles fanning that call out to every leaf underneath, however deep the nesting goes.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: computing total size over a file/folder tree recursively
Compare: Composite vs a flat collection with type-checking
slides.markdown:
The alternative to Composite is a flat list plus manual type checks.

| | Composite | Flat + type-checking |
|---|---|---|
| Adding a node type | Implement the interface, done | Update every isinstance/switch that walks the structure |
| Client code | One polymorphic call, no branching | Branches on type at every call site |
| Nesting | Arbitrary depth via recursion | Manual recursive logic re-invented per feature |
| Best for | Structures that can nest | A genuinely flat, single-level list |

**How to decide:** if the structure can ever nest — folders inside folders, menus inside menus — Composite pays for itself immediately; for a flat, one-level list, the extra interface may be overkill.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: leaf nodes forced to implement child-management methods they don't support
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "To keep one clean interface, File should implement add()/remove() just like Folder — it can just throw or no-op."

**Why it's wrong:** forcing `File.add(node)` to exist when a file can never have children violates the interface silently — callers see a usable-looking method and get a confusing runtime error, or worse, a silent no-op. It's a textbook interface-segregation problem: the interface promises a capability half its implementers don't have.

**Correct model:** keep `add`/`remove` on a narrower interface, or only on `Composite`, not the shared `FileSystemNode` base — so leaves never fake support they don't have. Code that adds children should be written against the type that can actually do it.

slides.sectionTitle: Where Composite shows up: UI component trees, org charts, menu systems
slides.markdown:
UI frameworks are Composite everywhere: a `Button` (leaf) and a `Panel` (composite containing other components) both implement `render()`, so a layout engine calls `.render()` on the root and the whole tree draws itself recursively. Org charts model the same way — an individual contributor and a manager with reports both answer `get_headcount()`, with a manager's answer summing everyone beneath them.

**When NOT to use it:** if your structure is genuinely and permanently flat — no nesting ever — the extra leaf/composite interface split adds ceremony without buying anything; a plain list is simpler.
